name: Abhirameswarar Temple, Thiruvamathur
deity: Shiva as Abhirameswarar (Azhagiyanathar), with the Goddess Muthambigai (Azhagiya Nayaki)
period: A Paadal Petra Sthalam of Nadu Nadu, sung by Appar, Sambandar and Sundarar (7th–8th century); Chola inscriptions from the 10th century
summary: Near Villupuram, the Lord who gave the cows their horns faces his Goddess from a temple of her own: two shrines, east and west, at a sthalam sung by all three Tevaram saints.

sections.history: Thiruvamathur is a village about 7 km north-west of Villupuram, and its name — Thiru-aa-mathur, the sacred town of the cows — carries the temple's best-loved legend. The temple of Shiva as Abhirameswarar is one of the 276 Paadal Petra Sthalams and one of the shrines of Nadu Nadu, and it is among the comparatively few sung by all three of the great Tevaram saints: Sambandar and Appar each left two pathigams here, and Sundarar one. The original shrine is believed to be Chola work; its inscriptions reach back to the tenth century, including a gift of gold in the reign of Parantaka I, with later records of Rajaraja I and Kulothunga I. The present main temple took shape with Vijayanagara-period patronage.
sections.architecture: Thiruvamathur is unusual in having two separate temples. Shiva's faces east; directly opposite stands the Goddess Muthambigai's own temple, facing west, so that the Lord and the Goddess face one another — and tradition points to an opening between the two through which they are said to behold each other. Within the main temple the lingam of Abhirameswarar is worshipped as the Lord who gave grace to the cattle, and Chola inscriptions run along the walls.
sections.legends: The sthala purana tells that in the beginning the cows had no horns and could not defend themselves. Kamadhenu, the wish-granting cow, led the herds to seek Nandi's help, and they worshipped Shiva here; pleased, the Lord granted them horns — and the place became Thiru-aa-mathur, the town of the cows. A local tradition also holds that Rama and Sugriva sealed their alliance against Ravana at this spot.
sections.festivals: Maha Shivaratri, the annual festivals of the Lord and of the Goddess Muthambigai, Navaratri and the monthly pradosham are the chief observances, kept with the customary Shaiva worship of the year; confirm dates locally.
sections.experience: The pleasure of Thiruvamathur is its double darshan: worship at Abhirameswarar's east-facing temple, then cross to Muthambigai's shrine and look back towards the Lord. In a farming village, a temple that honours the cattle feels close to daily life, and the shrine's five Tevaram pathigams — praise from all three saints — give it a quiet distinction.

visit.timings: Open daily in morning and evening sessions with a midday closure, as at most village temples of the region. Confirm current timings locally before visiting.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected — shoulders and knees covered; footwear is left outside before entering. Follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.photography: Photography is not permitted inside the sanctum; in the outer corridors, ask the temple staff before taking pictures, especially of rituals and the festival bronzes.
visit.gettingThere: Thiruvamathur lies about 7 km north-west of Villupuram on the road towards Thirukkovilur and Tiruvannamalai, with frequent buses and autorickshaws from Villupuram. Villupuram is the nearest major railway junction; Puducherry has the closest airport, and Chennai the nearest major international airport.
